# @aponiajs/devtools

> The opt-in devtools surface for a running AponiaJS application. A disabled registration mounts nothing; an enabled one mounts an Elysia plugin whose wildcard route sits in the application's own route table under `/__devtools`, on the address the application already answers, and serves an HTTP API there.

The package is a leaf: nothing in the framework depends on it. An application registers it and decides for itself whether the devtools mount at all — the framework never reads an environment variable to choose its own behaviour. **It requires Bun at runtime.** The surface is built on the runtime's own globals — `import.meta.dir` while the handler build resolves the Elysia the application installed, and `Bun.Glob` and `Bun.file` while `/aot` reads the project — so a Node process cannot serve this mount: `import.meta.dir` reads `undefined` there and a request through the mount fails in the handler build, answering `500` where the same boot answers `200` under Bun. The requirement belongs to the surface rather than to the framework around it, and an application that never registers this package never loads it. A configuration an application declares through `provideConfiguration` is the application's own read, not the framework's. There are two spellings that mount the same plugin: `DevtoolsModule.register({ enabled })` in a module's `imports`, and `devtoolsPlugin({ enabled })` in `AponiaFactory.create`'s `plugins` option. The option exists because `aponia build` lowers an `imports` entry only when it is a single identifier naming a declaration read from the project's own source: a registration returns a `DynamicModule` rather than a module class, so the module path declines the module that wrote it in every spelling, and the artifact the build leaves behind holds no declaration for that root — it is written without the module, or replaced with an empty record when the root was the only module a build could lower — so the boot refuses it and compiles the decorated graph instead: the registration mounts, and the declared-graph boot is given up. The option path trades that for a plugin no module declares, so nothing about it reaches the module graph, inspection, or a generated artifact.

## What this package exports

- [DevtoolsModule](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.ts): `register(options)` builds the module an application imports; a disabled registration is inert.
- [devtoolsPlugin](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.ts): the same plugin for `AponiaFactory.create`'s `plugins` option; a disabled registration answers `undefined`, which mounts nothing.
- [DevtoolsOptions](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.types.ts): the required `enabled` switch, the optional `capture` policy `/requests` records under — every option an opt-out, with `redact` empty by default because the tool shows what arrived — and the optional `logger` whose lines `/logs` records, the same object the application gives `AponiaFactory.create`, because the framework never exposes the logger it builds for itself. There is no `port` and no `host`: the surface is mounted on the application, so the application's own address is the only one it serves.
- [handleDevtoolsRequest](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/server/request-router.ts): the pure dispatcher every request goes through.
- [AponiaMetaPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/meta` payload, including the `contract` version a client checks first.
- [AponiaGraphPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/graph` payload, the compiled module graph with no `routes` key.
- [AponiaRoutesPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/routes` payload, every route the application answers with the binding that serves it.
- [AponiaRouteTracePayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/flow.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/flow` payload, the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws.
- [createLogBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-buffer.ts): the bounded log stream `/logs` publishes, and the capacity it retains.
- [recordLogger](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-tap.ts): records everything a `LoggerService` writes into a buffer, patching the logger in place and answering the stream that records it — one logger, one stream — or `undefined` when nothing could be installed on the logger, which is why a logger it cannot patch is never published as one. The stream it answers with states the levels the tap reached beside the buffer that records them, because an entry names only the level it was written at: without that list a level nothing was written at and a level the tap never installed into would read the same.
- [AponiaLogsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/logs` payload, the entries after one cursor, the cursor to poll from next, and the levels the stream reached.
- [AponiaRequestsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/requests` payload, the requests that reached the record after one cursor — one entry when a request arrives and one when it is answered, both carrying the request's `id` — and the cursor to poll from next.
- [AponiaBuildPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/aot.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/aot` payload — the graph the container compiled and the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, beside a build's per-handler verdicts for the project the application was started in.
- [createDevtoolsMcpServer, devtoolsMcpPath](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/mcp/mcp-server.ts): the embedded Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `/__devtools/mcp` (GET discovery, POST JSON-RPC 2.0).
- [createRequestBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/requests/request-buffer.ts): the bounded request record `/requests` publishes, and the capacity a registration retains.

## Behavior a consumer can rely on

- A disabled module registers no provider, mounts no plugin, and mounts no route.
- An enabled module registers a `PluginModule`, so its wildcard route and request hooks are merged into the application's own route table while it boots, beside the routes a controller mounted.
- The surface answers wherever the application answers: under `application.handle()` as well as `listen()`, because a route registered at bootstrap needs no `setup` — Elysia 1's `onStart`. An application route that claims a devtools path wins it, because the two owners sit in one table and the more specific route answers.
- The surface is part of the application's route table and is reachable wherever the application is, so `enabled` is how an application keeps it out of production: this is a development surface, and `/requests` records request headers and bodies by default with no warning. A registration names no port and no host, because the application already owns both.
- The surface stops with the application: `close()` removes its route with the application, so nothing outlives the listener that mounted it.
- `GET /__devtools/meta` reports the contract version — `3` in this release — the release that booted the application, the Elysia installed in the application's own tree (`null` when there is none), and which release supplied each artifact the boot adopted (`null` for one it did not).
- `GET /__devtools/graph` reports the graph the application compiled: its modules with their imports, controllers, providers, dependencies and exports, and its WebSocket gateways with their events. It describes the descriptor artifact's graph when the boot adopted one and the lowered decorated classes otherwise, and it carries no routes.
- `GET /__devtools/routes` reports the routes the application answers, read from the mounted table when the request arrives, so a route mounted after the boot appears too. Each route carries the method and path the table states, the module, controller and handler the boot recorded, the context fields its handler binds, and `source`: `"generated"` for a build-time invoker, `"compiled"` for the running platform's own binding, or `null` when no boot recorded the route, or when the record states a binding this release does not write. A route no record describes reports empty names rather than guessed ones.
- `GET /__devtools/flow` reports the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws, read from the mounted table when the request arrives. The stages a route's hooks and schema state come from that table; the stages its guards and interceptors state come from the compiled plan, because the platform lowered them into one `beforeHandle` and one `afterHandle` where their order is no longer legible, so each names the class it runs. A compiled hook is published as its parts and never as a hook stage; the installed Elysia 2 holds every hook a plugin or an instance-level declaration contributes as a bare function in the route entry's lifecycle array and stamps no scope, checksum, or `subType` on it, so none of those entries is identifiable and `/flow` publishes no contributed hook as a stage, while a hook a copy of Elysia does stamp an identity on is published as its own stage, that identity derived from its checksum rather than from a plugin name the route does not carry. Filters are a list beside the stages, never a stage in the chain. Which interceptor halves a route runs is the boot's own record, read from the instance the platform calls while the class resolved, so a half declared as a class field (`interceptBefore = () => {}`) is published like any other; a record that carries no such field — a copy of the platform older than this release — falls back to each class token's `prototype`, which answers for the class the token names rather than for the object the platform calls, so it is wrong in both directions: it publishes a half only when that token declares one there, which omits a field-declared half, and it states one for a token whose provider supplied an object of another shape — the object the platform calls in its place.
- `GET /__devtools/logs?since=<cursor>` reports what the application logged: the registration patches the logger the application passes as `logger` — the same object it gives `AponiaFactory.create` — and records every line into a bounded buffer from the moment the module registers, so the lines a boot writes about itself are included. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries, levels }` with each entry shaped `{ level, context, message, timestamp }`; `levels` names the `LoggerService` levels the tap reached on the logger it was handed, so a level the logger does not declare, or one whose assignment refused the patch, is stated as unreached rather than left to be inferred from an absent entry. A cursor older than the retained window answers what is retained and one ahead of every write answers nothing, so a poll is never an error, and the cursor never goes backwards. A registration with nothing to record from — an omitted option, `logger: false`, a level array the platform builds a logger from, or a logger object no level could be patched on — serves no `/logs` rather than an empty stream, because an empty stream would announce that nothing is being logged while an application that handed the factory a logger logs normally. The boundary is the number of levels patched, never where the first refusal landed: a logger the tap patched at least one level of is not that case — one that accepts a level's patch and refuses the next one's, or one whose `log` refuses while its `fatal` accepts — so the stream is served, each refusing level keeps the method it had, and every level after it is still patched. The levels reached are published rather than left to be inferred: `levels` names them, so a stream that never carries `debug` is told apart from one whose tap never reached `debug`. The one filter the stream cannot read is the logger's own — `LoggerService` has no notion of an enabled level, so a line the console would have suppressed is still recorded.
- `GET /__devtools/requests?since=<cursor>` reports the requests that reached the record and what answered them. One request writes two entries and both carry the same `id`, so a consumer groups by `id` and takes the last entry each request has in the window it reads — the answer wherever the answer is still there to read, which one configuration bounds: a consumer lagging more than one window behind never reads an answer FIFO eviction has already dropped; the first is written when the request arrives and states `status: null` and `durationMs: null`, which is this record saying it saw the request and read no answer for it — a plugin that answered from its own `request` hook before any later phase ran, for instance — rather than an invented status or a missing entry, and it states the path that arrived because no route has matched yet. Both hook phases run in mount order, so a plugin mounted ahead of the devtools registration that answers from its own `request` hook ends the request before this record's hook runs, and that request appears nowhere. The surface's own traffic is excluded too, and by path prefix rather than by route identity: `/__devtools` and everything under it is never recorded, which keeps a page polling `/requests` out of the window it reads — so an application route that claims a `/__devtools` path wins it and its traffic is unrecorded all the same. Everything is recorded by default and every option under `capture` is an opt-out, never a permission: an entry carries the `method`, the `path` — the route pattern that matched, or the path that arrived when none did — the `url` as it arrived, the `status`, the `durationMs`, the `timestamp`, the request's `headers`, and the `body` the route parsed, truncated at `capture.bodyLimit`, while a body this package cannot serialize is stored as `[unserializable]` rather than left out, because a missing `body` would read as a request that carried none, and a body that arrived as a literal JSON `null` is stored as the text `null` for the same reason. `error` carries the failure's message: what the answer published, or — for an unhandled failure the platform mapped — the exception that mapping answered, or — for an application-owned `5xx` an `HttpError` answers — the exception the context carries, whose `message` is the `detail` that response published. The status is the whole test: a `4xx`, an answer rather than a failure, carries none, and so does a `5xx` a handler built itself, whose body is the one the client already holds. The mapped failure is the one whose message comes from the exception rather than the answer: the mapping answers one fixed sentence for every such failure and its `Response` is not on the after-response context either, so the boot records the exception the mapping answered, and the entry publishes the same account `/logs` states for it, with no stack, both through one rendering — `@aponiajs/common`'s `formatLogValue`, which does not fold, so a message that itself spans lines is published with them — while the fold-to-one-line rendering is a different one, this package's own `oneLine`, which the row written for a failure of its own guard — the unread analysis — embeds, and which answers the literal `[unrenderable]` for any value whose read refuses, including a value the shared rendering still states — `{}`, or `[object Object]`; a value that refuses both the JSON form and the plain string form is stated as the literal `[unrenderable]` on both, because that rendering is total: it runs in the route's own `error` hook before the answer is built, and the logger call beneath it is guarded, so a refusal there is announced on `stderr` rather than costing the answer. A token passed as a query parameter is captured in `url`, which is a fact about the record rather than a defect in it: `capture.redact`, empty by default, replaces named headers with `[redacted]`. `durationMs` is measured from the moment the request reached this package's arrival hook to a reading the completion path takes before its first read of the context, so the route, the status, the parsed body — and the one microtask spent reading a readable `5xx` answer's published body — are outside it; the arrival hook's own URL and header capture remains inside, as does the pending entry's build and write because the opening stamp precedes both, and the field is not "the time the application spent on the route". A request that matched no route has no route identity — `path` carries the path that arrived, and `/routes` is the table that tells the two apart. The record belongs to one application rather than to a listener: two applications in one process, and two registrations, keep their own windows, and a second `listen()` continues the window the boot opened rather than beginning an empty one. A registration told to capture nothing still serves `/requests`, answering an empty record rather than no endpoint, and writes no arrival entry either. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries }` under the same cursor rules as `/logs`, except that its cursor counts entries rather than requests — one request writes two of them — so a poll is never an error and the cursor never goes backwards.
- `GET /__devtools/aot` reports what a build decided beside what the boot did with it. `graph` — the root the container compiled — and `invokers` — the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, with the refusal's own sentence and no `reason` key at all when there was no refusal — come from the boot record, so they are answered whether or not a project is on disk. `controllers` comes from `@aponiajs/cli`'s analysis of the project the application was started in — the source root `aponia.json` names, walked the way `aponia build` walks it — and gives each handler's verdict: `"generated"` when the emitter renders an invoker for it, `"compiled"` when it declines and the running platform keeps compiling it, with the emitter's own reason. A handler is one property key, however many route decorators it carries. The analyzer is imported on the first request to this endpoint and never at boot, and its result is cached for the life of the process, so an application that never polls this endpoint never loads `ts-morph`. A project the analysis cannot read — no `aponia.json`, no controller under the source root, a source root outside the project, two controllers sharing one class name, an analyzer that would not load — leaves `controllers` empty and reports the reason once under `Devtools`, while the boot's own facts are still answered; that report is guarded, so a logger that throws on it cannot turn the degraded half into a failed request. A project whose every handler was declined still reports those verdicts, because they are what the endpoint exists to explain. The endpoint is served only for a record that states the two boot facts it publishes; a record that does not is answered with `404` while every other endpoint this surface serves keeps answering. That is a different failure from a project the analysis cannot read, which still answers with the boot's half and an empty `controllers`.
- Every endpoint is a `GET`. Any other method answers `405` before the path is read, and a path the surface does not serve answers `404`.
